opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that a lot of what makes an assistant genuinely helpful isn't general world knowledge. It's context about *you*. A generic model knows a huge amount about the world, but it doesn't know what you were working on last Tuesday, which papers you've already read, who you've been emailing about a particular project, or what your preferences are when you ask for something to be done "the usual way."

When a model can draw on your own information, like your documents, your email, your calendar, your photos, and the code you've written, it can answer questions that a generic model simply can't. Say you ask, "What was that restaurant my friend recommended a few months ago?" or "Summarize where we landed on the design discussion for this system." Those aren't hard reasoning problems. They're retrieval-plus-understanding problems over *your* data. And once the model has that grounding, its general capabilities become much more valuable, because it's applying them to the things you actually care about.

There's also a compounding effect. The more the system understands your context, the less you have to spell out in every request. Today you often have to write a long prompt explaining your situation. With a personalized model, a lot of that is implicit, so interactions get shorter, more natural, and more like working with a colleague who's been on the project with you for a while.

Of course, you have to do this carefully. People need to be comfortable with how their data is used, have control over what the model can access, and trust that it's handled privately and securely. But if you get that right, I think personalized models with access to your information will feel qualitatively more useful than generic ones. It's the difference between asking a very smart stranger and asking a very smart assistant who actually knows you.

r001.rationale: The response describes using personal data and recalling past activity, but it does not raise the possibility of attending to a person’s entire lifetime of encountered information.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that a generic model knows a lot about the world, but it knows nothing about you. And so much of what makes an assistant actually useful is context. If I ask a colleague to help me prepare for a meeting, they know what projects I'm working on, who I'm meeting with, what we talked about last week. They don't need me to re-explain everything from scratch every time. A generic model is a little like a brilliant stranger. Every conversation starts at zero.

So if a model can see your email, your documents, your calendar, your past conversations, the questions you've been asking, then a lot of ambiguity just goes away. You can say "summarize where we are on that thing with the vendor" and it actually knows which thing and which vendor. You can ask it to draft a reply and it writes in your voice, with your level of formality, knowing the history of the thread. That's a qualitatively different experience from pasting in a bunch of context every time, which most people simply won't do.

The other piece is that the model can start to be proactive. If it understands your goals and your situation, it can notice things. It can say, you have a flight tomorrow and there's a conflict with this meeting, or this paper that just came out is relevant to the problem you've been stuck on. A generic model can't do that because it doesn't know what you care about.

Now, obviously this raises real questions about privacy and about how that information is stored and used, and I think those have to be taken very seriously. The right design is one where the user is clearly in control of what the model can see. But if you get that right, I think the gap between a model that knows you and one that doesn't will be very large. It's the difference between a tool and something closer to a true assistant.

r001.rationale: The response describes access to personal sources such as email, documents, calendar, and past conversations, but does not raise the possibility of attending to a person’s entire lifetime of encountered information.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of usefulness comes from having the right context. A generic model might know a tremendous amount about the world, but it doesn’t know what you’re working on, what you care about, or what you’ve already tried. You have to explain all of that every time you ask it something.

If you give a model access to information you want it to use—your documents, your email, your calendar—it can connect a general question to your particular situation. If you ask, “What should I prepare for tomorrow?” it could understand which meetings you have and identify the relevant material, rather than give you generic advice about preparing for meetings.

And that doesn’t necessarily mean training a separate model for every person. A lot of it is about bringing the right information into the model’s context, with you controlling what it can access. That makes it much more useful as an assistant.

r001.rationale: The response mentions access to personal documents, email, and calendar, but does not raise the possibility of attending to all information encountered over a person’s lifetime.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a generic model doesn’t have much context about you beyond what you put into the question. A personalized model could understand what you’re working on, what your preferences are, and what information is relevant to you—with your permission, of course.

If you ask, “What should I focus on today?” the useful answer depends on your commitments, the projects you’re involved in, and perhaps an email that arrived this morning. Without that context, you get fairly generic advice. With it, the model can help with your actual situation, and you don’t have to explain all that background every time.

r001.rationale: The response describes access to current personal context, such as projects, preferences, commitments, and email, but does not raise the possibility of attending to a person’s entire lifetime of encountered information.
